no_access.title: No access to the console
no_access.subtitle: This account is signed in, but it holds no administration permission.
no_access.subtitle_email: {{email}} is signed in, but it holds no administration permission.
no_access.alert_body: The console is opened by permissions, not by an account flag. Once a role carrying one is granted, sign in again so a fresh token carries it.

overview.title: Overview
overview.attention_description: Things that will break quietly if nobody looks at them.

attention.invitations_expired_one: {{count}} invitation has expired without being used.
attention.invitations_expired_other: {{count}} invitations have expired without being used.
attention.applications_inactive_one: {{count}} application is deactivated and cannot sign anyone in.
attention.applications_inactive_other: {{count}} applications are deactivated and cannot sign anyone in.
attention.secrets_expiring_one: {{count}} application has a client secret expiring within two weeks.
attention.secrets_expiring_other: {{count}} applications have a client secret expiring within two weeks.
attention.secrets_missing_one: {{clients}} is confidential and holds no usable secret, so it cannot authenticate at the token endpoint.
attention.secrets_missing_other: {{clients}} are confidential and hold no usable secret, so they cannot authenticate at the token endpoint.

overview.access_description: What this session holds in this application.
overview.access_note: Roles travel in the access token, so one granted since you signed in shows up after the next refresh. The API re-reads them on every request and is never out of date.
overview.activity_description: The last few entries of the audit trail.

users.title: Users
users.description: Every account on the service, newest first. Search matches on email and name.
users.empty_hint: Sign-up is invitation-only, so the first account arrives through an invitation.
users.no_matches_hint: Search matches on the email address and the display name.
users.account_description: The profile belongs to the person and is refreshed from whichever provider signed them in, so it is not editable here.
users.unverified_hint: No provider has confirmed this address yet, so an account cannot be linked to it by email alone.
users.enable_hint: A disabled account can neither sign in nor refresh a token.
users.disable_hint: Disabling revokes every session at once, so it takes effect immediately rather than at the next token expiry.
users.disabled: Account disabled, and its sessions revoked.
users.roles_description: What this account may do, and where.
users.roles_note: A role takes effect on the API immediately — permissions are re-read on every request — but the holder's own interface only sees it once their token refreshes.
users.identities_description: The provider accounts linked to this user.
users.sessions_description: One row per sign-in on one device in one application.
users.revoke_sessions_body: Sign {{email}} out of every application and device. Their refresh chains end immediately; they can sign in again right away.

avatars.title: Profile pictures
avatars.description: A picture somebody uploads is not published on its own: it is approved or refused here. While it waits, nobody can see it.
avatars.empty_body: When somebody uploads a picture it shows up here for you to review.
avatars.rejected: The image was refused and deleted.
avatars.reject_body: The image is deleted and the person sees the reason on their account. They can upload another one afterwards.
avatars.reason_placeholder: Optional: why it is not published

sessions.title: Sessions
sessions.description: Who is signed in right now. A session is one sign-in on one device in one application, so the same person may hold several.
sessions.revoke_body: End {{email}}'s session in {{application}}. The refresh chain dies immediately; the access token already issued stops working on its next request.
sessions.empty_hint: Revoked sessions are not listed here.

invitations.title: Invitations
invitations.description: Sign-up is invitation-only, so this is the allowlist: an address that is not here cannot create an account through either provider.
invitations.empty_hint: An invitation is an allowlist entry for an address, consumed the first time it completes a sign-in.
invitations.application_hint: Leave unset to let the address sign in to any application.
invitations.role_hint: Granted on top of whatever role the scope hands out by default.
invitations.created_unsent: {{email}} was invited, but no email went out — there was no login URL to point them at.
invitations.resent: The invitation was emailed to {{email}} again.
invitations.revoke_body: {{email}} will no longer be able to sign up. An account they already created is unaffected.

applications.title: Applications
applications.description: Every client that may start a sign-in at this issuer.
applications.register_description: A client id, where it may send people back to, and how it authenticates.
applications.empty_hint: Nothing can sign in until a client exists to sign in through.
applications.identity_description: How this client is named, and whether it may be used at all.
applications.client_id_hint: Lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores. This is what the client sends as `client_id`, so it cannot be changed afterwards.
applications.client_id_fixed: Fixed: every deployment of this client quotes it, and so does every token already issued.
applications.name_hint: Shown on the hosted sign-in screen, so the person can see what they are signing in to.
applications.active_hint: Deactivating stops new sign-ins at once. Tokens already issued keep working until they expire; revoke the sessions to end them now.
applications.urls_description: Where this client may send a browser, and which origins may call the API on its behalf.
applications.redirects_hint: Matched byte for byte, with no wildcards and no prefix matching — a trailing slash is a different URI. At least one is required.
applications.post_logout_hint: Where `GET /oauth/logout` may return the browser. Matched exactly, like the ones above.
applications.origins_hint: Extra browser origins allowed to call the OAuth endpoints cross-origin. A `https://*.example.com` pattern is accepted here, and matched on a dot boundary — this is the one field that takes one, because a preview deployment answers on a hostname that does not exist until it is deployed.
applications.oauth_description: How this client authenticates, and what it may ask for.
applications.auth_method_hint: `none` is a public client: it holds no secret and PKCE is the only thing binding an authorization code to the browser that asked for it. A browser application cannot keep a secret, so `none` is the right answer for every front-end.

auth_method.client_secret_post: Client secret in the request body
auth_method.client_secret_basic: Client secret in the HTTP Basic header

applications.pkce_hint: Can only be turned off for a confidential client, and exists for off-the-shelf relying parties that never implemented it.
applications.pkce_locked: Mandatory while this client is public: without a secret, PKCE is the only thing binding the code to the browser.
applications.grants_hint: The client may only use the grants ticked here. `client_credentials` authenticates the application itself rather than a person, and needs a secret.
applications.scopes_hint: The client may only ask for the scopes ticked here.
applications.scopes_all: Nothing ticked means every supported scope, which is what a client gets unless it is narrowed.

secrets.title: Client secrets
secrets.description: Only a hash is stored, so nothing here can be turned back into a usable value. A new secret is shown once, when it is issued.
secrets.public_body: It is a public client and authenticates with PKCE alone. Change the token endpoint authentication first — and only if it can actually keep a secret, which a browser application cannot.
secrets.label_hint: Optional, and only for telling two secrets apart in this list.
secrets.rotate_label: Rotate: give the existing secrets a deadline
secrets.rotate_hint: Several secrets can be valid at once, which is the point of rotating rather than replacing: every deployment gets a window to pick the new value up before the old one dies.
secrets.grace_hint: How long the current secrets keep working.
secrets.grace_zero: Zero ends them immediately, which is what a leaked secret calls for.
secrets.issued_once_title: This is the only time it is readable
secrets.issued_once_body: Only its hash is stored, so closing this dialog is the end of it. Copy it into the client now; if it is lost, issue another one.
secrets.copy_failed: The clipboard is not available here — select the value above and copy it by hand.
secrets.revoke_body: The secret starting {{hint}} stops working immediately. Any deployment still presenting it will fail to authenticate.
secrets.none_active: This client holds no usable secret, so it cannot authenticate at the token endpoint.

roles.title: Roles
roles.description: A role is a bag of permissions. Route guards check the permissions and never the role name, which is what makes a role freely re-definable.
roles.create_description: What it is called, where it applies, and which permissions it carries.
roles.empty_hint: Without a role, nobody holds a permission and the console is closed to everyone.
roles.identity_description: Two of these cannot be changed afterwards.
roles.slug_hint: Lowercase letters, digits, hyphens and underscores.
roles.slug_fixed: Fixed: it is what existing grants and every token already issued name this role by.
roles.scope_hint: A global role applies to every client application; a scoped one only where it was defined, so the same person can be an admin of one application and a plain user of another.
roles.scope_fixed: Fixed, for the same reason the slug is.
roles.default_hint: Every account that signs in within this role's scope gets it, without anybody granting it.
roles.permissions_description: Exactly what this role carries. Saving replaces the whole set rather than merging into it.
roles.delete_body: {{name}} is dropped, and with it every grant of it — the accounts that held it lose whatever it gave them, on their next request.

permissions.title: Permissions
permissions.description: Every capability a role can be given. Creating one grants nothing by itself: a permission is a string that travels in the access token, so defining one is how another service gets a capability of its own.
permissions.empty_hint: The auth service seeds the ones its own routes check; these are the rest.
permissions.slug_hint: Shaped `resource:action`, which is the convention the seeded ones follow.
permissions.slug_fixed: Fixed: it is what every route guard, every role and every issued token names this permission by.
permissions.delete_body_one: {{slug}} is deleted and detached from the {{count}} role holding it. The auth service refuses this for the slugs its own routes are guarded with.
permissions.delete_body_other: {{slug}} is deleted and detached from the {{count}} roles holding it. The auth service refuses this for the slugs its own routes are guarded with.

audit.title: Audit log
audit.description: Every sign-in, token issuance, revocation and administrative write, appended and never edited.
audit.empty_hint: Entries appear as soon as somebody signs in.
audit.no_matches_hint: The filters combine, so a narrow range and a specific event may have nothing in common.

settings.title: Settings
settings.description: How this authentication service behaves. Changes take effect on the next sign-in; nothing here touches an account that already exists.
settings.registration_open: Anybody who can receive mail at an address, or sign in with Google, gets an account on their first sign-in.
settings.registration_closed: Only an invited address can create an account. Everybody else is refused, without being told whether the address exists.
settings.registration_hint: Invitations keep working either way. Closing this again refuses the next sign-up, including a sign-in link that was emailed while it was open.
settings.closed: Registration is closed. Only invited addresses can create an account.
settings.read_only: You can read these settings but not change them. That needs the settings:write permission.
settings.turnstile_note: The sign-in screen is protected by Cloudflare Turnstile wherever the deployment has a key pair configured — which is what keeps an open registration from being an invitation to a script. That is deployment configuration rather than a setting, so it is not changed from here.
